stimulus.text:
| City | Region | Approximate population at its height |
| Tenochtitlan (Mexica) | Central Mexico | About 200,000 |
| Cahokia (Mississippian) | Mississippi River valley, near present-day St. Louis | About 20,000 |
stimulus.source_note: Approximate figures; Cahokia about 20,000 at its peak in the 1200s and Tenochtitlan about 200,000, consistent with standard estimates (see grounding).

source: original; fresh authoring; population figures approximate, see grounding
stem: How does maize farming relate to the growth of both Tenochtitlan and Cahokia?

options.text: Maize farming kept both cities small by limiting their stored food.
options.misconception: Reverses the link: surpluses fed growth, not smallness.

options.text: Maize farming mattered in Mexico but played no part in Cahokia.
options.misconception: Denies Cahokia's farming, though the city depended on maize surpluses.

options.text: Both cities grew large mainly because European traders supplied them with food.
options.misconception: Credits Europeans who arrived centuries after both cities grew.

options.text: Maize surpluses fed large populations in both cities, in different regions.

rationales.A: Maize surpluses fed growth in both cities, so farming did not keep them small.
rationales.B: Cahokia depended on maize surpluses from the river valleys just as Tenochtitlan did in Mexico.
rationales.C: Both cities grew centuries before Europeans arrived, so European traders cannot explain their size.
rationales.D: Maize surpluses fed about 200,000 people in Tenochtitlan and about 20,000 in Cahokia, in two different regions.
rationales.general:
1. Name the link. Maize farming produced more food than a family needed, a surplus.
2. Follow the surplus in Mexico. It fed Tenochtitlan, a city of about 200,000 people.
3. Follow the surplus north. It fed Cahokia, a city of about 20,000 in the Mississippi valley.
4. Connect the two. One crop, carried on the same surplus, fed large cities in two different regions.
Remember: a surplus is the bridge between farming and cities, so trace the food first.
